title: Routing: mirror sampled requests to shadow targets (fail-open + strict timeouts)
author: Ravi Menon
description: Summary: Adds sampled request mirroring (“shadow traffic”) in the data plane router. For eligible requests, we deterministically decide whether to mirror, dispatch a best-effort shadow request to one or more configured shadow targets, and always return the control response to the user. The shadow path is strictly fail-open: any failures in mirroring must not impact the user path, latency SLOs, quotas, or error rates. Motivation: This is the core data-plane capability for the Shadow Traffic tool for eval metrics. Control plane will attach a shadow policy to routes/rollouts; the router enforces it with timeouts and circuit breaking. Scope: (1) Add mirroring hook in router request handling for chat/completions/embeddings; (2) enforce strict time budgets for shadow dispatch + response capture; (3) backpressure + circuit breaker integration so we stop mirroring when downstream is unhealthy; (4) telemetry counters for attempted/queued/sent/failed/timeouts (cardinality-safe); (5) unit + integration tests covering fail-open, streaming behavior, and multi-target policies. Design notes: Mirroring is executed after we have the control request fully validated and admitted (so shadowing cannot be used to bypass auth/limits). Shadow requests reuse the same normalized request payload, but we drop/override selected headers per policy (e.g., no customer auth propagation; add x-redwood-shadow: true; scrub x-request-id). Shadow calls are non-blocking with a dedicated worker pool and bounded queue; on saturation we drop shadow work and emit a counter. Timeouts: The shadow dispatch budget is capped at 25ms wall time in the request thread; response capture is done asynchronously with a hard 2s timeout per target (configurable, but max-capped). If the shadow call exceeds its budget or errors, we record outcome and move on. Streaming: For streaming requests, we mirror only the initial normalized prompt + generation params. We do not stream shadow tokens back through the router; the shadow request uses non-streaming mode by default (policy can opt in later). This avoids coupling user token streaming to the shadow path. Security/PII: This PR does not add any prompt/response storage; it only emits low-cardinality counters and attaches a “shadow dispatch outcome” to the in-memory trace context. Full shadow pair artifacts are handled by the telemetry/retention workstream (ENG-5404 / ENG-5411). Rollout: Guarded behind feature flag shadow_traffic_mirroring (default off). Also requires a route policy with sampling > 0 and at least one shadow target. Test plan: Added unit tests for sampler determinism and header scrubbing; integration tests using router test harness to validate: (a) shadow target 500/timeout does not affect control response; (b) queue saturation drops shadow work; (c) circuit breaker opens after consecutive failures and stops mirroring; (d) per-target timeout enforcement; (e) streaming requests do not block on shadow. Observability: Added counters under router.shadow.* and a histogram for shadow dispatch enqueue latency. No high-cardinality dimensions; labels are limited to route_id (capped/bucketed), request_type (enum), outcome (enum), and shadow_target_slot (small int). Risks: Minor CPU overhead in hot path for sampling decision + enqueue; measured in benchmark harness at +0.2–0.4% CPU in router at 1% sampling. Failure modes: If shadow targets are slow/unhealthy, we drop work and open the breaker; control path should be unaffected. Follow-ups: (1) integrate deterministic request fingerprinting once ENG-5403 lands; (2) wire shadow telemetry event emission (ENG-5404); (3) revisit streaming shadow semantics with Applied ML once scoring pipeline is stable.

conversation:
Mina Haddad (review): Can you confirm we never wait on shadow completion in the request thread? Also, what’s the maximum work we’ll do before returning the control response?
Ravi Menon (author): Correct—request thread does (1) sampling decision, (2) best-effort enqueue with a 25ms cap across all targets, and then returns control response as usual. Shadow execution + capture happens in workers. If queue is full or budget is exceeded we drop and increment router.shadow.dropped.

Sean Gallagher (review): Need stronger guarantees on fail-open and explicit guardrails. Add circuit breaker thresholds and ensure we never propagate shadow errors into control traces as “error” severity.
Ravi Menon: Added breaker (open after 50 consecutive failures per target, half-open after 60s) and scoped logging to debug with metrics for outcomes. Control span remains success; shadow outcome is attached as an attribute (shadow_outcome=timeout/error/dropped) for internal debugging.

Logan Wright (review): Please keep metric labels cardinality-safe. Do not include customer_id, model_id, or raw route name. Also ensure route_id is capped/bucketed.
Ravi Menon: Updated metrics to use route_id_hash_bucket (0-1023) + request_type + outcome + shadow_target_slot only. No model identifiers.

Benji Okafor (review): Header scrubbing: ensure x-forwarded-for and auth headers are not copied. Also need a policy allowlist for what we do forward.
Ravi Menon: Implemented explicit allowlist (content-type, user-agent (optional), x-redwood-traceparent) and a denylist for auth/cookies/x-forwarded-*; added unit tests.

Chloe Martin (review): The console backend expects a stable notion of “shadow target slot” for aggregation; please avoid emitting arbitrary target strings.
Ravi Menon: Done—targets are indexed by policy order and emitted as small int slot.

CI: Initial run failed due to flaky integration test timeouts in the harness (reran with deterministic fake clock). Final run is green.

Outcome: Approved by Mina/Sean/Logan/Benji/Chloe; merged squash to main.
release_notes: Data plane: adds feature-flagged shadow request mirroring with strict fail-open behavior, bounded queueing, and circuit breaker protections. No customer-visible behavior changes unless enabled via policy + flag.
